analogy.p: Think of a power as a button on a machine that does a job to a number. Raising to the power 2 is a "squarer", and the power 1/2 is its undo button, the square rooter, because pressing both (adding the indices 2 × 1/2 = 1) leaves the number as it was. A negative index is a "flip" lever that turns a number into its reciprocal, and flipping twice gets you back to where you started, just as the reciprocal of a reciprocal is the original number. The picture breaks down because a real machine runs one button at a time, whereas index notation packs the whole job into one exact value, and the analogy does not explain why a negative base cannot always take a root.

bullets: **Negative index** means **reciprocal**: a^(−n) = 1/aⁿ. It does **not** produce a negative answer.
**Fractional index** means **root and power**: a^(m/n) = (ⁿ√a)ᵐ. The **denominator is the root** and the numerator is the power.
All the index laws you know still work, with the indices added, subtracted or multiplied as fractions or negatives.
The two skills are usually combined in exam questions, with a typical order of working: flip, root, power.
Typical question styles: evaluate (2–3 marks), simplify an algebraic expression (2–3 marks), write as a single power (2 marks), solve an index equation (2–3 marks).
Mastering the recall of squares, cubes and powers of 2, 3, 5 and 10 from the previous topic makes this topic quick and accurate.
This is Higher tier content, so it appears on all three papers at grades 6 to 9.
core.h: What the specification asks and why it matters
core.p: At Higher tier you must be able to **use and interpret negative and fractional indices**, extending the index laws that you already know for positive integers. In practice this means evaluating expressions such as 4⁻², 27^(1/3), 8^(2/3) and (27/8)^(−2/3) without a calculator, writing roots and reciprocals as powers (for example 1/√x = x^(−1/2)), simplifying algebraic expressions, and solving equations in which the unknown is in the index. The topic is a core non-calculator skill, and it supports surds, standard form with small numbers, algebraic fractions, calculus-style thinking in later study and exponential graphs.

bullets: Powers of 10: 10⁻¹ = 0.1, 10⁻² = 0.01, 10⁻³ = 0.001; the index tells you the position after the decimal point.
A negative index in the **denominator** moves to the top: 1/a⁻ⁿ = aⁿ, so 1/2⁻³ = 2³ = 8.
a⁻¹ is simply the reciprocal of a: 4⁻¹ = 1/4 and (2/5)⁻¹ = 5/2.
With a coefficient the index only affects its own base: 3x⁻² = 3/x², whereas (3x)⁻² = 1/(9x²).
Negative number bases keep the usual sign rules: (−2)⁻³ = 1/(−2)³ = −1/8.
Do not write 2⁻³ = −8 or −6; the answer is 1/8 = 0.125.
Write answers as a fraction unless a decimal is requested; fractions are exact.
core.p: A **negative index** tells you to take the **reciprocal** (1 divided by the number) of the same power with a positive index: a^(−n) = 1/aⁿ. For example 2⁻³ = 1/2³ = 1/8, and 10⁻² = 1/100 = 0.01. The sign of the index controls where the term goes (the bottom of a fraction), not whether the value is positive or negative. A positive base always gives a positive answer, however negative the index. This idea is the same one used in standard form for small numbers, where 4 × 10⁻⁵ = 4/100 000 = 0.00004.

bullets: **Cancelling**: a²/a⁵ = 1/a³ and also a²⁻⁵ = a⁻³, so a⁻³ = 1/a³.
**Ladder of powers**: 2³ = 8, 2² = 4, 2¹ = 2, 2⁰ = 1, 2⁻¹ = 1/2, 2⁻² = 1/4, 2⁻³ = 1/8, with ÷ 2 at each step.
The values approach 0 but **never reach it or become negative**, so 2ˣ > 0 for all x.
Combined with a⁰ = 1: a⁻ⁿ × aⁿ = a⁰ = 1, so a⁻ⁿ is the number you multiply aⁿ by to get 1, which is its **reciprocal**.
Using this: 3⁵ × 3⁻² = 3³ = 27 (add indices) and also 243 × 1/9 = 27, a good check.
The graph of y = 2ˣ for negative x lies above the x-axis and slopes up to the right towards 1 at x = 0.
This links to division in algebra: x³ ÷ x⁵ = x⁻² = 1/x².
core.h: Why a negative index means reciprocal
core.p: It helps to see where the rule comes from, because understanding makes it harder to forget. The division law says a² ÷ a⁵ = a²⁻⁵ = a⁻³. But you can also cancel: a² ÷ a⁵ = (a × a)/(a × a × a × a × a) = 1/a³. Both expressions describe the same quantity, so a⁻³ = 1/a³. The pattern of powers of 2 shows the same thing: moving one step down the ladder 8, 4, 2, 1 divides by 2 each time, so the next values are 1/2, 1/4, 1/8. The extension of the ladder below 2⁰ gives the negative powers.

bullets: A whole number is a fraction over 1: 4⁻¹ = (4/1)⁻¹ = 1/4.
Mixed numbers must be converted to improper fractions first: (1 1/2)⁻² = (3/2)⁻² = (2/3)² = 4/9.
Negative signs in the base stay: (−2/3)⁻³ = (−3/2)³ = −27/8.
Decimal bases: (0.5)⁻³ = (1/2)⁻³ = 2³ = 8; convert to a fraction first.
Check using the pattern: flipping twice returns the original, so ((2/3)⁻²)⁻¹ = (2/3)².
Common error: flipping and also making the answer negative; (2/3)⁻² is positive.
In exam answers show the flip: (2/3)⁻² = (3/2)² = 9/4, which earns the method mark.
core.h: Negative indices applied to fractions: flip
core.p: When the base is a fraction, the negative index **flips** the fraction (swaps numerator and denominator) and you then apply the positive power: (a/b)⁻ⁿ = (b/a)ⁿ. For example (2/3)⁻² = (3/2)² = 9/4. This works because the reciprocal of a/b is b/a, so the negative index asks for the reciprocal of (a/b)ⁿ, which is (b/a)ⁿ. Always flip **first**, then square or cube; this keeps the numbers positive and avoids fractions inside fractions such as 1/(4/9).

bullets: **a^(1/n) = ⁿ√a**: the denominator tells you which root. Example: 16^(1/4) = 2 since 2⁴ = 16, and 32^(1/5) = 2.
Fractions: (4/9)^(1/2) = 2/3 and (8/27)^(1/3) = 2/3 (root top and bottom).
Proof idea: (a^(1/n))ⁿ = a^(n × 1/n) = a¹ = a, so a^(1/n) is the number whose nth power is a.
Algebra: x^(1/2) = √x and (x^(1/3))³ = x.
Know the common roots: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100, 121, 144 for squares and 1, 8, 27, 64, 125, 1000 for cubes.
Negative numbers have no real square root, but ∛(−8) = −2, so (−8)^(1/3) = −2 is allowed.
core.p: A **fractional index with numerator 1** means a root: a^(1/2) = √a, a^(1/3) = ∛a, and in general a^(1/n) = ⁿ√a. The reason is that a^(1/2) × a^(1/2) = a^(1/2 + 1/2) = a¹ = a, so a^(1/2) is the number that multiplies by itself to give a, which is exactly what a square root is. Similarly three factors of a^(1/3) multiply to a¹, so a^(1/3) is the cube root. This is why fractional powers are the natural way to write roots in algebra.

bullets: **a^(m/n) = (ⁿ√a)ᵐ**: denominator is the root, numerator is the power.
**Root first** gives smaller numbers; doing the power first still works but needs bigger arithmetic.
If the base is not a perfect power the answer is a surd or decimal; GCSE non-calculator questions always use perfect powers.
Common error: treating 8^(2/3) as 8² ÷ 3 = 64/3 or 8 × 2/3. The fraction is an index, not a multiplier.
Remember: **denominator = root, numerator = power**. A memory aid is "the bottom is the root".
core.p: A fractional index with numerator m and denominator n means **take the nth root and raise to the power m**: a^(m/n) = (ⁿ√a)ᵐ = ⁿ√(aᵐ). The two forms always give the same value, but it is much easier to take the **root first**, because this keeps the numbers small. For example 8^(2/3) = (∛8)² = 2² = 4, whereas 8² = 64 and ∛64 = 4 is correct but harder without a calculator. The law behind it is the power of a power law: a^(m/n) = (a^(1/n))ᵐ, since 1/n × m = m/n.

bullets: Step 1 (negative): take the reciprocal; for a fraction, flip it.
Step 2 (denominator): take the nth root of the base (of the numerator and denominator separately for a fraction).
Step 3 (numerator): raise to the power m.
Do not mix up the order: the negative sign flips the **whole** answer, it does not change the root or power.
core.p: Many exam questions put the two ideas together, for example 16^(−3/4) or (27/8)^(−2/3). The reliable method has three steps in a fixed order: **flip** (the negative sign gives the reciprocal), **root** (the denominator n), **power** (the numerator m). Doing the steps in this order, and writing each line, avoids mistakes with reciprocals of fractions. Worked: 16^(−3/4) = 1/16^(3/4) = 1/(⁴√16)³ = 1/2³ = 1/8. Another: (27/8)^(−2/3) = (8/27)^(2/3) = (∛(8/27))² = (2/3)² = 4/9.

bullets: **Power of a power**: (x^(2/3))³ = x^(2/3 × 3) = x².
**Brackets with a coefficient**: (27a⁹)^(2/3) = 27^(2/3) × a⁶ = 9a⁶ because ∛27 = 3 and 3² = 9, and 9 × 2/3 = 6.
**Negative index in a product**: (8x⁶y⁻³)^(2/3) = 4x⁴y⁻² = 4x⁴/y².
When subtracting indices that give a negative, the term goes to the denominator: x^(1/2) ÷ x³ = x^(−5/2) = 1/x^(5/2).
Use common denominators: 1/3 + 1/2 = 5/6, so x^(1/3) × x^(1/2) = x^(5/6).
Check with a number: choose x = 4 and test, e.g. 4^(1/2) × 4^(3/2) = 2 × 8 = 16 = 4² ✓.
core.h: The index laws with fractional and negative indices
core.p: All the index laws hold for fractional and negative indices: aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ, aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ, (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ. When the indices are fractions you add, subtract or multiply them as fractions, using a common denominator for addition and subtraction. In algebra the coefficient is handled separately from the letters: (8x⁶)^(1/3) = 8^(1/3) × x^(6 × 1/3) = 2x². Writing each step (cube root of 8 is 2, and 6 × 1/3 = 2) is the safest way to protect marks. The laws can also be used to simplify products such as x^(1/2) × x^(3/2) = x².

bullets: A fraction like 5/x² is 5x⁻²; a root in the denominator, 4/√x = 4x^(−1/2).
Combine: x ÷ √x = x¹ ÷ x^(1/2) = x^(1/2) = √x.
Write each term separately for sums: 2/√x + √x³ = 2x^(−1/2) + x^(3/2); you cannot combine terms with different indices.
When writing as a single power, give the index as a fraction (like 3/2) or decimal (1.5) if the question allows it.
core.h: Writing roots and reciprocals as powers
core.p: A very common algebra task is to rewrite an expression using index notation: √x = x^(1/2), ∛x = x^(1/3), ⁿ√(xᵐ) = x^(m/n), 1/x = x⁻¹, 1/xⁿ = x⁻ⁿ and 1/√x = x^(−1/2). Each rewriting uses just the two rules from this topic. You may be asked to write an expression in the form k xⁿ, where k and n are numbers. Take care that the coefficient stays outside: 3/x² = 3x⁻², not (3x)⁻². This skill is useful before differentiating or integrating at A-level, so it is a worthwhile habit.

bullets: To undo a power xᵖ, raise both sides to the **reciprocal** power 1/p: x^(3/2) = 8 → x = 8^(2/3) = 4.
x⁻² = 1/9 → x² = 9 → x = 3 or x = −3 (both squared give 9).
Check by substitution: 4^(3/2) = (√4)³ = 8 ✓.
If bases look different, convert to a common base first (4 = 2², 8 = 2³, 9 = 3², 27 = 3³).
When the unknown is a power of a power, multiply the indices before equating.
core.h: Solving equations with the unknown in the index
core.p: To solve equations such as 2ˣ = 1/16 or 9ˣ = 1/27, write both sides as **powers of the same base** and then **equate the indices**. Negative indices handle the fractions, because 1/16 = 2⁻⁴ and 1/27 = 3⁻³. Fractional indices handle the roots, so x^(3/2) = 8 means x = 8^(2/3) = 4, found by raising both sides to the reciprocal power 2/3. The method relies on the fact that for a positive base other than 1, if aˣ = aʸ then x = y. Show the base-matching line clearly; it is the method mark.

bullets: Type fractional powers with brackets: 27 ^ (2 ÷ 3) = 9.
Use the fraction template (if available) for the index, or the decimal 0.75 for 3/4 only when the decimal is exact.
Never type 8^2/3; it gives 64/3 = 21.3…, not 4.
Use the x⁻¹ key for reciprocals, and the a b/c key to keep fractions exact.
Exact answers on non-calculator papers: 1/8 not 0.125 (both are acceptable if exact), but 0.3333 is not.
Always write the unrounded calculator display before rounding.
Estimate: 10^(1/2) lies between 3 and 4 because 3² = 9 and 4² = 16 (actual 3.162…).
Standard form: 6.4 × 10⁻³ = 0.0064, which uses the negative-index pattern for small numbers.
core.p: A scientific calculator has a power key (x^y, ^ or xʸ), a reciprocal key (x⁻¹), and √ and ∛ keys. On calculator papers you can check your work, but you must enter fractional indices with **brackets**, for example 16^(3÷4) typed as 16 ^ (3 ÷ 4), otherwise the calculator takes 16^3 ÷ 4. Non-calculator papers expect exact fractions rather than decimals, so 2⁻³ is written as 1/8. Use the calculator to confirm, not to replace, the method, because the method gets the marks if you slip on the keys.

bullets: Pitfall: a^(−n) is **not** −aⁿ and not −n a.
Pitfall: a^(m/n) is **not** a^m ÷ n; the fraction is the index of one power.
Pitfall: (a + b)^(1/2) is not a^(1/2) + b^(1/2); roots do not split over addition.
Link: standard form 5 × 10⁻³ = 0.005 uses negative indices.
Link: exponential decay y = a × 0.5ᵗ has a graph like y = 2⁻ᵗ, falling towards zero but never reaching it.
Link: surds: 8^(1/2) = √8 = 2√2 uses the product law inside the root.
Extension: a^(1/n) works for all positive a and positive integer n; for even n and negative a the result is not a real number.
Extension: zero index with fractions still gives 1: (2/3)⁰ = 1.
core.h: Common pitfalls, links to other topics and extension
core.p: The most common errors with this topic are mixing up the roles of the numerator and denominator in a fractional index, forgetting to flip the whole fraction for a negative index, and making answers negative when the index is negative. Link ideas to the rest of the course: **surds** (√a = a^(1/2)), **standard form** (negative powers of 10), **algebraic manipulation** (simplifying with x^(1/2)), **exponential graphs** (y = aˣ), **compound decay** (multiplier ^ n with decay). Developing a systematic three-step method (flip, root, power) turns a source of lost marks into a reliable five-mark source.

exam: **Command words**: "Work out" and "Evaluate" want an exact value (a fraction is fine); "Simplify" and "Write as a single power" want an expression like x^(5/6); "Solve" wants a value of x.
**1-mark** questions are basic evaluations such as "Write down the value of 2⁻³" (1/8) or "Work out 81^(1/2)" (9).
**2-mark** questions such as "Work out 8^(2/3)" award a mark for the correct cube root (2) and a mark for the final value 4; show the root step.
**3-mark** questions such as (27/8)^(−2/3) award marks for the flip (8/27)^(2/3), the root 2/3, and the answer 4/9.
Always lay out the method: flip, root, power. Even if the final answer is wrong, a correct flip or root earns method credit.
Algebra questions (e.g. simplify (8x⁶)^(1/3)) give a mark for the numerical part and a mark for the power of x, so deal with both separately: 2x².
In index equations, write the common-base line: 9ˣ = 3²ˣ, 1/27 = 3⁻³, then equate indices; the final answer is x = −3/2.
Give answers as exact fractions or integers on non-calculator papers; decimals only if they are exact (0.125).
When asked to "write as a power of x", give the index; if it is negative, do not convert it to a fraction unless asked.
Check an answer by substitution or estimate (e.g. 8^(2/3) must be between 8^(1/2) ≈ 2.8 and 8¹ = 8).
Calculator papers: use brackets for fractional indices; the question might ask you to confirm "show that" an exact value, so show the working, not just the display.

mistakes.r: 4⁻² = 1/4² = 1/16; a negative index means reciprocal, not negative.
8^(2/3) = (∛8)² = 2² = 4; the denominator is the root, the numerator is the power.
27^(1/3) = ∛27 = 3; a power of 1/3 is a cube root, not division.
3x⁻² = 3/x²; the index applies only to x, not to the 3.
(x³)^(1/3) = x^(3 × 1/3) = x¹ = x; multiply the indices.

summary: At Higher tier you must evaluate, simplify and solve with negative and fractional indices: a^(−n) = 1/aⁿ (the reciprocal) and a^(m/n) = (ⁿ√a)ᵐ (denominator is the root, numerator is the power), using the same index laws and the order flip, root, power. It is a core non-calculator skill that supports surds, standard form, algebra and exponential graphs.

terms.d: An index below zero, which means the reciprocal of the same power with a positive index: a^(−n) = 1/aⁿ.
1 divided by a number; the reciprocal of a is 1/a and of a fraction a/b is b/a.
An index written as a fraction, for example a^(m/n), meaning the nth root raised to the power m.
The inverse of a power; the nth root of a is the number which, raised to the power n, gives a.
A number that multiplies by itself to give the original; a^(1/2) = √a.
A number which, used three times as a factor, gives the original; a^(1/3) = ∛a.
The value written ⁿ√a, equal to a^(1/n).
Rules for combining powers of the same base: add indices to multiply, subtract to divide, multiply for a power of a power.
The number that is raised to a power.
The numerical factor multiplying a variable, for example 3 in 3x⁻².
Write an expression in a more compact form, for example as a single power of x.
Writing different numbers as powers of the same number, for example 8 = 2³ and 4 = 2², so equations can be solved by equating indices.
If aˣ = aʸ then x = y (for a > 0, a ≠ 1); the step used to solve index equations.
An irrational root left in exact form, such as √2 or 3√5.
Another word for index or power.

steps: (b) Denominator 4 is the fourth root: ⁴√81 = 3 (since 3⁴ = 81). Numerator 3 is the power: 3³ = 27.
Cube root of top and bottom: ∛8 = 2 and ∛27 = 3, so (2/3).

worked.q: Simplify (8x⁶y⁻³)^(2/3), giving your answer without negative indices, and write 1/√x ÷ x² as a single power of x. [4 marks]
steps: Second part: 1/√x = x^(−1/2). Dividing by x² subtracts 2: −1/2 − 2 = −5/2.
